terms.gloss: oppose, be against, go against (someone’s wishes)
terms.grammar: verb, first conjugation, deponent, with the dative
evidence: Cic. Verr. 2.5.81 (Lewis & Short): hujus libīdinī adversārī
terms.comment: Opposition in opinion or will, which is what English usually means; Lewis & Short notes that resistere and obsistere are rather resistance by action. Frequent in Cicero.

terms.grammar: verb, first conjugation, intransitive; with the dative or absolutely
evidence: Cic. Fam. 1.2.2: cōnsulēs neque concēdēbant neque valdē repugnābant
Caes. B.C. 1.32 (Lewis & Short): Catōne ācerrimē repugnante
terms.comment: Literally to fight back, of soldiers defending themselves; so to put up resistance to a proposal. Of things compared, to be inconsistent with each other, mostly in Cicero (Lewis & Short).

terms.gloss: stand in the way of, withstand
terms.grammar: verb, third conjugation, with the dative
evidence: Cic. Cat. 3.17 (Lewis & Short): omnibus ejus cōnsiliīs obsistere
terms.comment: Literally to plant oneself in someone’s way (Plautus); so to block a plan.

phrases.latin: Redūc uxōrem, ac nōlī adversārī mihi.
phrases.english: Take your wife back, and don’t go against me.

phrases.latin: ego sum animō lēnī nātus: nōn possum adversārī meīs.
phrases.english: I was born soft-hearted: I can’t stand up against my own family.

phrases.latin: cōnsulēs neque concēdēbant neque valdē repugnābant
phrases.english: the consuls neither gave way nor put up much opposition

sources: Lewis & Short: adversor · Lewis & Short: repugno · Lewis & Short: obsisto
